articles.title: European Court of Human Rights orders Turkey to free Osman Kavala
articles.summary: Philanthropist and activist Osman Kavala has spent almost a decade in jail over charges rights groups say are politically motivated.
articles.body:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ordered Turkey to immediately release Osman Kavala, an activist and philanthropist who has been detained in prison for almost a decade.

Kavala was sentenced to life behind bars in 2022 for charges related to nationwide protests in 2013 and a failed coup attempt three years later.

Since his initial arrest and detention in 2017, rights groups and Kavala himself have maintained that the charges against him are politically motivated.

The ECHR on Tuesday ruled that his continued detention was unlawful and that his rights to a fair trial, freedom of expression and association had been violated.

"The measures taken against the applicant... had been predominantly motivated by an ulterior purpose, namely, to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender, and to silence him," the court said in its ruling , external .

The court also found that Kavala's aggravated life sentence amounted to "inhuman and degrading treatment".

Rights advocates and opposition groups say President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has increasingly weaponised the judiciary to target critics and rivals.

The court said Kavala's case had exposed a "systemic problem" in Turkey of the "detention and prosecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists", adding that there were "structural shortcomings which affected the guarantees of independence and impartiality of the judiciary".

The Turkish government has insisted the country's courts are independent.

Turkish activist sentenced to life in prison

The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West Published 25 November 2021

The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West

Kavala, 68, became a symbol of a government crackdown on civil society in Turkey following his arrest in October 2017.

He and others were accused of orchestrating and financing anti-government protests in 2013, which started in Istanbul's Gezi park before spreading across Turkey.

The demonstrations posed the first serious challenge to the rule of Erdogan, who was Turkey's dominant prime minister at the time and became its directly elected president the following year.

Human rights group Amnesty International says prosecutors falsely alleged that the Gezi park protests were an attempt to overthrow the government.

In 2019, the ECHR demanded Kavala's immediate release, describing his detention as arbitrary and politically motivated. Turkey did not implement the ruling.

He was initially acquitted in February 2020 but within hours was rearrested on new charges of being part of a failed military coup in 2016.

His acquittal over the Gezi Park protests was overturned in January 2021, and he was sentenced to life in prison in April 2022 - a conviction now declared "null and void" by the ECHR.

Reacting to the latest ECHR ruling, Amnesty International's Eve Geddie said: "This obstruction of justice must end. Turkey's authorities, including judicial and prosecutorial, must act to free Osman Kavala immediately and unconditionally."

Kavala was born in Paris and educated in the UK. Before being thrust to prominence, he ran a cultural centre.

Erdogan has previously accused Kavala of being an agent of the Hungarian-born US billionaire George Soros.

Turkey has refused to comply with the two previous ECHR rulings on Kavala's case, and it is not clear whether Ankara will implement the court's third binding ruling.

The case remains one of the most serious recent flashpoints between Ankara and Strasbourg.

The Council of Europe oversees how its 46 member states execute ECHR rulings. It has the power to freeze a country's membership or suspend its voting rights if it is found to have seriously violated the rule of law.

Even though Turkey has failed to comply with several key ECHR decisions, it remains a founding member, engages with the system and has not broken ties.

A meeting of the Committee of Ministers in mid-September is likely to prioritise the Kavala case, but it remains to be seen whether it will debate harsh punitive measures.

articles.title: 'Zero self-awareness': Indian-origin professor slams viral video of woman welcoming parents at US airport triggering wheelchair row
articles.summary: US News: Videos of Indians using wheelchairs at international airports surface on social media from time to time. This time, a video of an Indian woman apparen.
articles.body: Videos of Indians using wheelchairs at international airports surface on social media from time to time. This time, a video of an Indian woman apparently welcoming her parents at Dallas-Fort Worth Airport in Texas went viral as the mother was seen emerging from the airport in a wheelchair. But later she was walking."Dallas Fort Worth airport needs to publish its recovery statistics. Arrives needing a wheelchair and two airport employees. Leaves walking after all five suitcases have been handled. Remarkable medicine," an X post sharing the video commented sarcastically. It also mentioned that the video was on a public platform.The video went viral amid massive backlash targeted at Indians and Indian parents, while many explained why the wheelchairs are not only meant for disability but also for travel anxiety, long waiting, changes in schedules etc.Indian-origin professor Gaurav Sabnis slammed the 'scammy mindset' and observed that the woman didn't even think twice before posting the video. "Shows how normalized the scammy mindset has become in our culture in recent years. This woman didn't even have a thought before posting it that she was giving evidence of her parents using wheelchairs as a "jugaad". That this could go viral for that fact. Zero self-awareness," Prof Sabnis noted.Sabnis also countered factors like 'travel anxiety' and said that people from other countries too face anxiety, but wheelchairs are mostly abused by Indians. "Flaunting it on social media shows the extent of the moral rot in today's Indian elite," he commented. "Aren't there older adults from other countries flying places?" he asked."I've been traveling multiple times a year for many years and this wasn't common in 2012 for example where you still had a lot of senior citizens landing at Newark for their kids. This is a jugaad actively spread using Whatsapp and social media," he later explained.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Former South Wales Police officer charged with raping and strangling woman in Swansea
articles.summary: Rikki Hall, 33, was on duty in Swansea when he allegedly attacked the woman, the police watchdog said.
articles.body:
A former police officer allegedly raped and strangled a woman while on duty, according to the policing watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said ex-constable Rikki Hall had been charged with two counts of rape and one count of non-fatal strangulation.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

He will appear at Bristol Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The IOPC said its investigation began in February 2024 following a mandatory conduct referral from South Wales Police.

"A substantial file of material was submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in February 2025 and, following further lines of enquiry being undertaken, charges were authorised by the CPS," it added.

articles.title: ‘Please don’t do this’: Dave Ramsey says to ditch this one household expense keeping Americans from becoming wealthy
articles.summary: Want to build wealth? Start by never financing a car again, Dave Ramsey says.
articles.body:

When it comes to the relationship one has with their car, you come first; The car comes second.

That's the advice financial guru Dave Ramsey offered Carl from New York when the 29-year-old father called into The Ramsey Show (1).

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

JPMorgan sees gold hitting $5,000/oz by Q4 — and savvy investors are protecting their wealth with a tax-advantaged Gold IRA. Get your free guide from Priority Gold

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

"Love yourself enough not to go into car debt," Ramsey told him. "If you want to be middle class, stay in car debt. You will never build wealth because it will suck the bone marrow out of your money."

Carl added that he recently got a pay bump from $85,000 to a possible $95,000 after six months and his current Honda isn't worth fixing. He has $20,000 in savings for a new car, but the one he wants costs $25,000.

"Don't celebrate your new job with a car payment. That's kind of dumb," Ramsey said. "You have $20,000 and an $85,000 job in New York City. You can go buy a $20,000 car and not a dime more," Ramsey said.

He told Carl his budget is whatever he sells the Honda for, plus the $20,000. According to a recent study, $100,000 in Manhattan is equivalent to about $30,362 — the lowest purchasing power of any city on a list of 20 (2).

Ramsey linked the affordability crisis to high car payments. A Bank of America report found that in 2025, nearly a quarter of households live paycheck to paycheck (3).

"Ford Motor Company screwed you. Lexus and Toyota screwed you," he said. "They got you to go far in debt because you had to have something shiny with a toxic plastic smell."

Ramsey used Carl's situation to make a broader point, citing internal research of more than 10,000 millionaires showing that 84% credited ditching car payments as key to building their wealth.

Ramsey suggested that Carl stop caring about what people think and move away from seeing his car as a status symbol.

"Decide who you want to impress. People you're likely never going to meet, or your grandchildren," he added. "Because you can change your family tree if you don't impress the people at the stoplight," Ramsey said.

"You are upgrading so far from the hooptie you've been driving, you ought to be dancing in the streets with that $20,000, acting like you have got a new Porsche," Ramsey added.

articles.title: The $20,000 dorm room has arrived. Why Gen Z is taking its home away from home so seriously.
articles.summary: TikTok loves the monograms and custom decor. Students say the real appeal is having a tiny corner of campus that feels like theirs.
articles.body:
For Julie Beth Fox and Kari Cabale, designing the perfect dorms for their newly minted college freshmen was an act of love.

The two stay-at-home moms from Nashville first met when their kids, now in their 20s, were in kindergarten. They became fast friends, going to church together and supporting one another as they raised their combined six children. After years of coming up with fun and easy crafts and designing decor for various high school events, they were eager to flex their creativity to make their kids' rooms perfect, but within reason.

"I wanted her to be confident, and have all the things," Fox tells me of her oldest daughter, who attended Mississippi State. "But I also knew that I was going to set the precedent with her, and if I blew the budget, I would have to continue that. I spent a lot of time thinking it can be elegant, it can be elevated, but it doesn't have to be expensive."

The friends began helping out other moms in their community who found the process of outfitting a dorm room a bit overwhelming, and they loved it so much they decided to start their own company, which they named Petal and Pine Dorm Design . They weren't sure what to expect when they officially launched in June, but the response and the number of clients they have worked with have been beyond their wildest expectations.

"We're kind of overwhelmed and blown away, to be honest," Fox says. "We just thought we'd throw it out there, and we were quite surprised."

Their success is likely due to the fact that dorm design, as a concept, has gone viral. Gone are the days when you'd roll up at your first college living space with an extra-large twin "bed in a box" from Bed, Bath & Beyond and maybe a cute lamp or a poster and call it a day. Now, a perfectly aesthetic, curated dorm can take weeks or even months to create. Some students go all out, spending big bucks to make it perfect.

Beautifully decorated dorms have been trending on social media, particularly TikTok, for a few years, but this year they've hit the cultural zeitgeist in a new way. After a few TikTok videos of elaborately designed dorms being revealed to their gasping undergrads went viral, the internet at large began to obsess over the perfectly curated color schemes, matching monogrammed pillows and, one can assume, hefty price tags for touches like custom built-ins and a shelf to hold their designer bags .

The fascination follows a broader online trend toward a cultural obsession with big public university culture in the South (see: # RushTok ). But the dorm designers I spoke to also believe that the desire for a custom and comfortable room is unique to the current generation of college students. Sure, they want to post beautiful photos to social media to keep up with their peers, but they also value their personal space in a different way.

"Having a beautiful dorm space helps me to feel more at home," Kamryn Hall, a 19-year-old sophomore at Florida State, tells me. When she's not studying, Hall creates content geared toward other college students and has been sharing her journey of designing her second-year dorm room.

"It isn't necessarily about the aesthetics," she says about her choice to invest in her space, which includes a pink ruffled duvet and a custom LED name sign . "It's more about self-expression and getting to showcase everything that I love in a space that's mine and having some feel of individuality, especially when you're in a shared space."

Shannan Bower has worked as an interior designer in Fort Worth, Texas, for 18 years, and added dorm services to her repertoire several years ago. She thinks the fact that Gen Z spent so much time indoors and at home during the pandemic gave them an appreciation of " how your environment can affect the way you feel."

"It's not just about making something pretty for social media," she tells me. "Students want personalization, comfort and a space they can come back to at the end of a long day and genuinely feel at home in. A dorm doesn't have to just be four walls, a bed and a few posters anymore."

Still, for those of us who grew up in that "four walls and a few posters" era, the juxtaposition between what we had and what we see online now can be hilariously stark. Content creator Melanie Ressa, who is 35, jokingly joined the conversation on Instagram by posting a photo of her old dorm, which had one piece of "art": a beer pong poster. She's endlessly fascinated by the rooms she keeps seeing online, she says, because she considers college to be a time when your life should be anything but curated.

"My hot take is that these girls have their entire lives to be adults," she says. "Dorm rooms are not supposed to be perfectly crafted design spaces. What happened to the display of liquor bottle trophies, stolen street signs and posters bought from Spencer's?"

Then there's the debate over costs. After videos of "dorm reveals" from one designer, Shelly Gates of Mississippi, went viral on TikTok last year, she revealed to People that her services can cost up to $20,000 for a custom room. But Fox and Cabale say you don't have to spend a fortune, and most people don't. The extremes may be going viral, but their clients are shopping on Amazon and at HomeGoods (their consultations start at just $100).

Bower advises her clients to invest the most in the items that will be functional for the most important parts of college life: studying and sleeping (what did you think I was going to say?).

"Invest in comfortable bedding and a good mattress topper because sleep is incredibly important for a college student," she says. "Make sure you have functional storage so you're not constantly living in clutter, and create a study space where you can actually spread out and focus."

Fox and Cabale have found that creating a beautiful living space, with the help of parents and/or a decorator, is often a cathartic experience for their young clients. Leaving home and attending college, after all, is a huge life change, and Fox likes to believe that making something cozy and chic can ease jitters for both moms and daughters before they step into the next chapter.

"We feel like it's giving the moms [a chance to] bridge that gap between them being at home and launching them," she says. "It's also giving the girls a lot of confidence and comfort in their new space. … They're really proud of what they're creating."

articles.title: China warns US of retaliation if Trump's 'Economic D-Day' sanctions hit their Iran oil trade
articles.summary: China News: China has warned that it could take retaliatory measures if the United States significantly expands secondary sanctions targeting Chinese companies do.
articles.body: China has warned that it could take retaliatory measures if the United States significantly expands secondary sanctions targeting Chinese companies doing business with Iran, according to reporting by the Financial Times.The warning came after the Trump administration on Monday announced new sanctions targeting companies in Hong Kong and mainland China as part of a broader crackdown on Iran's oil trade. The measures, however, did not target major Chinese financial institutions, FT reported.A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday that Beijing would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights and interests, while reiterating China's opposition to what it described as unilateral sanctions lacking a basis in international law or United Nations Security Council authorisation.The spokesperson also called for de-escalation and a return to dialogue and negotiations.China is Iran's largest oil customer, with Chinese buyers accounting for about 90% of Iran's oil exports. While China's state-owned refiners largely comply with US sanctions on Iranian crude, smaller private refiners, known as "teapots", continue to import and process Iranian oil.The United States has sanctioned some of those refiners this year, but Beijing has instructed Chinese companies not to comply with such measures.The prospect of broader US secondary sanctions comes at a sensitive point in US-China relations. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet in Washington next month, with the leaders expected to discuss extending a one-year truce in their trade dispute.Wang Dong, a senior scholar at Peking University, told FT that Beijing would defend its national interests if Washington moved ahead with broader sanctions, though he said it remained unclear whether the US threat was serious or a negotiating tactic.Zhu Feng, an international relations expert at Nanjing University, told the newspaper that China was also keen to see the conflict between the United States and Iran de-escalate.Zhu said continued restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz were putting additional pressure on the global economy and could pose a greater risk to China because of its dependence on Middle Eastern oil supplies."From a Chinese perspective, we don't want to get involved in a US-Iranian fight," Zhu told FT.Chinese officials have also stepped up diplomatic contacts in the Middle East. President Xi Jinping recently met Jordan's King Abdullah II, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi held talks with his Kuwaiti counterpart, with Iran and the Gaza war among the issues discussed, according to the Financial Times.Zhu said China's message to Tehran was that Beijing wanted peace talks to continue.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘No downside’: Warren Buffett trusts 2 key assets for his grandkids — and says the income will likely jump for decades
articles.summary: Buffett’s decades-old bets reveal a simple formula: Buy productive assets at the right price, then let their income and value compound over time.
articles.body:

Warren Buffett is best known as one of the greatest stock market investors of all time.

But some of the investments he has spoken most glowingly about aren't stocks at all.

In a letter to Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.B) shareholders, Buffett reflected on two personal investments he had made decades earlier — both far outside his usual world of publicly traded companies.

While not as famous as Berkshire's stock holdings, Buffett has expressed unwavering confidence in these investments.

"The two investments will be solid and satisfactory holdings for my lifetime and, subsequently, for my children and grandchildren," he wrote (1).

He also projected that the income from the two investments "will probably increase in the decades to come."

The answer reveals a lot about how the legendary investor thinks about building wealth that can last for generations.

The first opportunity appeared in 1986, after a bubble in asset prices had burst in the Midwest.

Buffett paid $280,000 for a 400-acre property about 50 miles north of Omaha — considerably less than the amount a failed bank had previously lent against it.

The Oracle of Omaha admitted that he "knew nothing" about operating a farm. But his son had a passion for farming, and Buffett was able to learn about the farm's production of corn and soybeans and its operating expenses.

Buffett then calculated that the normalized return from the farm would be 10%. He also believed that productivity would likely improve over time and that crop prices would increase. He highlighted that "both expectations proved out."

It didn't seem to be a hard decision to make, as he remarked, "I needed no unusual knowledge or intelligence to conclude that the investment had no downside and potentially had substantial upside."

That confidence paid off. Buffett noted that the farm had tripled its earnings by 2014 and was worth five times more than what he paid.

articles.title: Tyrone Noling: Gov. Mike DeWine to decide fate of Ohio death row inmate claiming innocence
articles.summary: Now the fate of the convicted double murderer, whose case has attracted support from Kim Kardashian and other celebrities, is in the hands of Gov. Mike DeWine.
articles.body: The Ohio Parole Board recommended Tuesday that a prisoner who has spent 30 years on death row for two murders he says he did not commit should have his sentence commuted to life in prison with the possibility of parole as early as 2029. The recommendation landed on Gov. Mike DeWine’s desk a week after Tyrone Noling asked the board for a full pardon. Now the fate of the 54-year-old Noling, whose bid for exoneration has garnered celebrity support from Kim Kardashian and actors Hilarie Burton and Jeffrey Dean Morgan, is in the hands of an outgoing Republican governor who, as a state senator, co-sponsored the legislation that reinstated capital punishment in Ohio in 1981. Since then, DeWine has had a change of heart, and in June he called on lawmakers to eliminate the death penalty, saying “the moral justification I had for voting for the death penalty simply no longer exists.” “We are encouraged that the Parole Board has taken a step towards recognizing the gross injustice Tyrone Noling has endured for decades,” said Brian Howe of the Ohio Innocence Project, one of Noling’s attorneys. “We hope Gov. DeWine will pardon Tyrone and allow an innocent man to go home at last.” DeWine has the power to pardon Noling, but he can also reduce his sentence or stay the execution to provide more time to pursue a legal remedy. One of the eight parole board members who took part in this case, former prosecutor Shontell Walker, was in favor of granting Noling a pardon, according to the board’s recommendation. Five were in favor of commuting his sentence and two were opposed. Noling, whose case has been the subject of documentaries and true-crime podcasts, has said he won’t accept a commutation of his sentence to life without parole. Typically, death row inmates aren’t allowed clemency hearings until they have an execution date. Noling doesn’t have one. And during his appearance before the parole board, his lawyers argued that he had nothing to do with the murders of an elderly couple. Prosecutors, however, have insisted that Noling is an unrepentant killer who at age 18 was part of a gang that did a string of robberies in Portage County, where he gunned down Bearnhardt and Cora Hartig, both 81, on April 5, 1990, inside their home in Atwater Township. Bearnhardt Hartig was shot three times and his wife five times with a .25-caliber automatic handgun. Their house had been ransacked. Noling was convicted on the strength of testimony from three other members of the gang who were 14, 15 and 16 at the time. They later retracted their statements, saying that police pressured them to name Noling as the shooter. While aggravated burglary charges brought against Noling were dropped in 1992, a grand jury reindicted him in 1995 for the Hartig murders. Noling was sentenced to death in 1996, even though no physical evidence tied him to the crime and no murder weapon was ever found. While Noling languished on death row, the Innocence Project lawyers uncovered law enforcement notes that pointed to three other potential suspects, including Dan Wilson, who was executed by lethal injection in Ohio in 2009 for the 1991 murder of a young woman. The Ohio Innocence Project lawyers wrote in court documents that the accused man’s original defense team was not aware, during his murder trial, that Wilson’s foster brother had told police that Wilson had bragged about killing the Hartigs. Also, Noling’s defense attorneys were aware that DNA testing on a cigarette butt found by detectives on the Hartigs’ driveway did not place Noling — or any of the three other teens — at the scene at the time. But they weren’t aware of a June 1991 blood-typing lab report that concluded that the cigarette could have been smoked by somebody like Wilson. Noling also got a boost from former Portage County Sheriff Ken Howe, now 83, whose department spent over two years reviewing the case but refused to hand it over to prosecutors because no weapon or physical evidence linked Noling and the other teenagers to the crime. It was the local prosecuting attorney and his investigators who secured the grand jury indictment against Noling. In an interview with The Associated Press, Howe said that there were red flags when police were investigating Noling for the slayings and the evidence that has accumulated since then has convinced him that neither Noling nor the other members of the alleged robbery gang were involved in the double murder. “I believe that these boys were, and are, innocent,” he said.

articles.title: British police arrest 5 more in fatal weekend crash; 17 now charged
articles.summary: British police said they arrested five people in their probe of a crash that killed seven people, bringing the number of people arrested to 17.
articles.body:
Aug. 25 (UPI) -- British authorities said they arrested five people Tuesday in their investigation following a weekend crash that killed seven people, bringing the total number of people arrested to 17.

The new arrestees include three people -- ages 16, 18 and 21 -- facing charges of of participating in an organized crime group; a 55-year-old arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender; and a 23-year-old accused of making threats to kill, The Guardian reported.

The announcement comes one day after police in Cleveland, which serves the Teesside area of northeast England, announced the arrests of 12 people Monday, identifying those detained as nine men and three women between the ages of 19 and 61.

They were detained on a range of offenses, including allegations of participating in organized crime, possession of an offensive weapon and drug-related crimes.

Two of those arrested Monday appeared in court -- Kai Beattie, 19, on a charge of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and Cameron George, 26, charged with drug offenses and possession of criminal property.

The suspects were detained over the weekend in a wide-scale investigation following a collision early Saturday involving a Volkswagen Passat and a police vehicle on the A66, resulting in the deaths of the five occupants of the Passat and two officers in the police vehicle.

Authorities were initially alerted early Saturday to reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously in Middlesbrough. A Volvo XC60 was allegedly seen ramming properties, while a Volkswagen Passat was believed to be associated with the Volvo. Police said both vehicles were operating with cloned license plates.

Police later spotted the Passat and pursued it for nearly 7 minutes before the Passat entered the A66 at South Bank, traveling against traffic, prompting the pursuing police vehicle to end its case.

However, seconds later, at 3:39 a.m., the Passat collided with a second police car, which was traveling in the correct direction, authorities said .

The deceased officers ere identified as Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38. The deceased occupants of the Passat were named as Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Jakub Matusiak and Michael Robert Cahill.

"The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect," Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said Monday in a statement.

The BBC reported Tuesday that the Passat belonged to a man who lived in one of the houses that had been rammed by the Volvo. After the vehicle hit the home, the man's son, Worthy, and five others got into the Passat and drove off.

Fox said they have a duty to investigate the "serious criminal activity" that led to the fatal crash and bring those responsible to justice, though it was not clear how those detained were involved.

"Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organized crime," Fox said.

articles.title: China, India hold border talks, agree to continue search for boundary settlement
articles.summary: BEIJING, Aug 25 (Reuters) - China and India agreed on Tuesday to continue dialogue and seek a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement" of their...
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug 25 (Reuters) - China and India agreed on Tuesday to continue dialogue and seek a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement" ‌of their border issue after talks between senior diplomats in ‌Beijing.

The world's two most populous nations, both nuclear powers, share a roughly 3,800-km (2,400-mile), largely undemarcated ​and disputed border in the Himalayas.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and India's National Security Advisor Ajit Doval had "comprehensive, in-depth, friendly and candid" discussions on border affairs and bilateral ties, China's foreign ministry said in a statement.

Wang said China-India ‌relations were no longer ⁠only of bilateral importance but carried global and strategic significance, saying the two neighbours should strengthen communication and reduce ⁠their differences.

The Indian Embassy in China confirmed in a post on X that the two sides had reviewed bilateral ties and had discussed ways to ​further expand ​cooperation and maintain stability and peace ​in border areas.

Ties between Beijing ‌and New Delhi have gradually improved in recent years following a deadly 2020 border clash, which led to a four-year military standoff before a disengagement agreement was reached in October 2024.

Last year Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China for the first time in seven years, in a sign ‌of a thaw in relations. More recently, ​a fresh border-related dispute triggered sharp diplomatic ​exchanges between the two rivals.

"Both ​sides should learn from historical experience, place the border ‌issue in an appropriate position in ​bilateral relations, and ​move forward without stagnation, regression, or deviation," Wang was quoted as telling Doval at Tuesday's meeting.

The two countries have agreed to hold ​the next round of ‌border talks in India in 2027, the Chinese statement added.

(Reporting by ​Beijing Newsroom, additional reporting by Bipasha Dey in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Alex Richardson and Gareth Jones)

articles.title: Florida voters have approved $35 million to buy and transform 5.8 miles of underused railroad into a trail that will form part of an 11.4-mile greenway and help close a gap in a planned 400-mile trail network
articles.summary: US News: Voters in the coastal Florida city of Bonita Springs have approved a $35 million general obligation bond, clearing the way for the local government to.
articles.body: Voters in the coastal Florida city of Bonita Springs have approved a $35 million general obligation bond, clearing the way for the local government to buy a key 5.8-mile stretch of unused railway. The ballot decision unlocks the missing central section of the wider 11.4-mile Bonita Estero Rail Trail (BERT). The project will also help close an important gap in the planned Florida Gulf Coast Trail, a 400-mile network that is intended to run across Southwest Florida. The referendum was held during the 18 August primary election. It allows the city council to issue up to $35 million in general obligation bonds with a 30-year repayment period. According to public election filings, $28.6 million will be used to buy the 5.8-mile inactive railway corridor from the Fay family, owners of the Seminole Gulf Railway. The rest will pay for engineering, design and the first stage of construction from downtown Bonita Springs.Completing the regional puzzleThe vote removes the final financial hurdle to buying the full 11.4-mile railway corridor, which covers about 180 acres across Southwest Florida. Neighbouring authorities had already committed money to secure their parts of the line. The Village of Estero to the north pledged $19.8 million to buy nearly four miles of track, while Collier County to the south committed $11.6 million for its 1.5-mile section. The combined purchase price agreed by the three jurisdictions is $60 million, about 20 per cent below the property's total appraised value. Because Bonita Springs lies between Estero and Collier County, its approval was seen by conservation groups as the key step needed to secure the entire corridor. "With the positive vote from Bonita Spring residents, we have the final piece in place for the purchase of the rail corridor for BERT," said Deb Orton, President of Friends of BERT, in a statement released through the Trust for Public Land. "Our next step is to complete the due diligence efforts that move us closer to the finalization of the purchase in October. The voters have given the Bonita Springs City Council a clear mandate they sought when they voted to place the referendum on the August 18th ballot for consideration."Cost and local debateThe $35 million bond will be repaid through local property taxes over 30 years. Financial estimates from PFM Financial Advisors show that the measure will add between $49 and $88 a year to the property tax bill for an average home valued at $441,137. Supporters, including the Naples Pathway Coalition, said this works out to about $4.75 a month per household. The project received strong support from local businesses and conservation groups, but there was also opposition before the vote. Some homeowners living next to the unused tracks raised concerns about privacy and security because of increased public access. Others questioned the cost of the project or suggested keeping the corridor available for possible light rail in the future. City leaders, however, argued that turning the abandoned railway into a paved path for walkers and cyclists would provide greater public benefits. They pointed to improved pedestrian safety, better regional connections and potential benefits for local businesses.A wider conservation projectThe Trust for Public Land (TPL), a national non-profit focused on land conservation and public parks, has played a major role in the project. TPL worked with city officials, the Naples Pathway Coalition and Friends of BERT volunteers on the corridor's valuation and public campaign. "Today, Bonita Springs voters made a bold endorsement to invest in a better future for their community," said Doug Hattaway, Southeast Region Conservation Director at Trust for Public Land. "Voters have resoundingly authorized its City Council to fund the corridor's purchase along with significant construction funding of the 5.8-mile Bonita Springs portion of the longer 11.4-mile rails-to-trails project involving also the Village of Estero to the north and Collier County to the south." The completed 11.4-mile trail will give runners, walkers and cyclists a new regional route while also connecting with the planned 75-mile Paradise Coast Trail, which is expected to stretch from Marco Island to South Lee County. The Paradise Coast Trail will then connect with the larger Florida Gulf Coast Trail, a planned 400-mile route linking communities from Naples towards the Tampa Bay area. With voters now approving the bond, city officials and project partners are conducting environmental checks and completing property assessments before the purchase is formally closed. The transaction is expected to be completed in October. Design work for the first paved sections in central Bonita Springs is expected to begin soon after the purchase is finalised.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Fortescue defended keeping an executive at work during a harassment investigation; days later it reversed course and suspended the employee
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Fortescue is facing renewed scrutiny over workplace conduct as an external investigation into allegations involving a senior executive runs alongside .
articles.body: Fortescue is facing renewed scrutiny over workplace conduct as an external investigation into allegations involving a senior executive runs alongside separate legal action brought by former employees. The mining company has confirmed that law firm MinterEllison is examining the allegations, while the executive remains employed as the inquiry continues. At the same time, a class action filed in July alleges broader workplace misconduct, including sexual harassment. The case follows similar proceedings involving BHP and Rio Tinto, putting workplace culture across some of Australia's biggest mining companies under growing attention.Fortescue's own annual figures add another layer to the story, with reported psychosocial breaches falling during the latest financial year. But those numbers cover a wider range of workplace concerns and cannot be treated as a direct measure of sexual misconduct. The separate investigations, court cases and internal reporting figures show how difficult it can be to assess workplace conduct through any single set of numbers.Fortescue has hired MinterEllison to investigate allegations against an unnamed senior executiveFortescue confirmed that MinterEllison had been engaged to examine allegations concerning the unnamed senior executive. The company has also sought outside legal and governance advice about how the matter should be handled while the inquiry continues.Gus Pichot, Fortescue's energy chief, said during an earnings call that the company believed it was following the appropriate process. The executive remains employed while the investigation is taking place.That arrangement means the allegations have not yet been resolved. The investigation is intended to establish what happened and whether any workplace rules or standards were breached.The allegations were first reported by the Australian Financial Review earlier in August. Fortescue has not publicly identified the executive involved.98 psychosocial breaches, with 11 dismissals over misconduct recordedThe investigation comes alongside Fortescue's annual disclosure of workplace conduct figures. The miner recorded 98 psychosocial breaches during the latest financial year, a 20% fall from the previous year.The category covers a range of workplace concerns rather than sexual harassment alone. It includes matters such as ethical issues and other incidents that can affect employees' psychological wellbeing.Fortescue said 11 employees had been dismissed for breaches of its code of conduct involving discrimination and sexual harassment. Its internal findings included 13 cases of inappropriate sexual contact, 10 cases of sexual harassment and one case classified as sexual assault.âSexual harassment, unlawful discrimination and any behavior that makes people feel unsafe have no place at Fortescue.âAs reported by Australian Financial Review (AFR), the company employs 16,154 people. Those figures provide a broader picture than the investigation involving the senior executive. They cover cases dealt with across the organisation during the financial year and do not indicate the outcome of the current inquiry.Mining's long-running workplace problemSexual harassment has remained a difficult issue for Australia's resources industry, particularly in Western Australia, where mining is a major employer and workplace culture at remote sites has faced scrutiny for years.A state inquiry into sexual harassment in the resources sector began in 2021. Its findings brought greater attention to complaints about inappropriate behaviour and the difficulties workers can face when reporting misconduct in workplaces where power structures can be pronounced.The issue has not been confined to Fortescue. BHP, the world's largest mining company by market value, reported 380 sexual harassment complaints in its latest financial year, an 11% reduction from the previous year. It also said 109 employees had been dismissed for sexual harassment and 22 for racial harassment.BHP's workforce, including contractors, numbers more than 84,000 globally, so its figures cover a much larger employee base than Fortescue's.Rio Tinto sees Care Hub reports climb, highlighting the limits of comparisonsReportedly, Rio Tinto has reported a different trend in the number of matters reaching its employee support system. The miner recorded 702 incidents through its Care Hub during 2025, a 24% increase from the previous year. The service deals with a broad range of harmful or disrespectful workplace behaviour, including harassment, rather than focusing solely on sexual misconduct.The figures from the three mining companies cannot be read as a direct league table. Their reporting systems, definitions and workforce sizes differ, and an increase in reports can reflect changes in reporting behaviour as well as changes in the underlying level of misconduct.A fall in complaints does not necessarily mean every form of harmful behaviour has declined, just as a rise can sometimes indicate that employees have become more willing or able to report what they experience.Western Australia has seen a fall in reported casesAs reported by Reuters, WorkSafe Western Australia also points to a reduction in incidents reported to the state regulator. WorkSafe recorded 28 incidents involving sexual assault and harassment during the first six months of 2026. That compares with 113 incidents across the whole of 2025 and 421 in 2022.The regulator linked the decline to the work of a specialist team established after the state inquiry. The team has expanded the regulator's capacity to respond to reports involving sexual harassment and assault.The figures cover reports received by the regulator and should not be taken as a measure of every incident occurring across the state's workplaces. Many cases may never reach a regulator.Fortescue faces legal action as its senior executive misconduct probe continuesFortescue is also facing legal action over alleged workplace misconduct. A class action filed in July alleges misconduct including sexual harassment and sex discrimination. The potential damages have not yet been specified.The case was brought by law firm JGA Saddler, which has also filed class actions against BHP and Rio Tinto over alleged workplace misconduct. Those proceedings, launched in late 2024, remain before the courts. The legal cases and Fortescue's internal figures are separate from the investigation now being conducted by MinterEllison. The external inquiry concerns allegations against a particular senior executive, while the class action addresses broader claims about workplace conduct.For Fortescue, the immediate issue is therefore being handled on two fronts: an investigation into allegations involving a senior figure and continuing legal scrutiny over wider workplace practices.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US Streamers News: Case Dylan Baker, known online as CaseOh, had a pretty normal working life before the internet changed everything for him. He was doing maintenance wo.
articles.body: Case Dylan Baker, known online as CaseOh, had a pretty normal working life before the internet changed everything for him. He was doing maintenance work with his father in rural Arkansas, handling things like plumbing and mowing lawns. Streaming was something he had wanted to do since his early teens, inspired by creators like Nadeshot and the early OpTic Gaming scene. But his first attempts at making videos did not really go anywhere. Then came September 2022. Baker started uploading batches of funny NBA 2K23 clips to TikTok, timing them around the release of new versions of the game. The move worked way faster than expected. Within 48 hours, he had gained more than 10,000 followers, and on September 11, he went live on Twitch for the first time. Just two years later, the same creator was standing at The Game Awards, winning Content Creator of the Year.CaseOhâs first big break came from NBA 2K23 TikToksThe TikTok strategy became the first real turning point. Instead of slowly building an audience, Baker pushed several short, energetic clips around NBA 2K23. The sudden follower growth gave him a reason to move those viewers toward Twitch.His early streams were not exactly running on a perfect setup either. Because of limited internet infrastructure in rural Arkansas, he famously had to use a mobile hotspot for some broadcasts. Still, the growth kept coming. By November 2022, less than two months after starting, he received an invitation to the Twitch Partner Program.His audience helped turn CaseOh into a variety streamerNBA 2K was only the beginning. Baker eventually moved into indie games, simulators, low-budget horror titles and Roblox. Games like Contraband Police and Supermarket Simulator became part of the variety format that defined his streams.A huge part of the appeal was his interaction with chat. Viewers regularly threw food-related jokes at him, including lines like âBuilt like a 1x1 Lego pieceâ and âCase-a-dilla.â His mock-rage reactions and quick ban-hammer moments became a recognizable part of the streams.CaseOh went from Arkansas maintenance work to The Game AwardsOn December 12, 2024, the journey reached its biggest point yet. At The Game Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, Baker won Content Creator of the Year.He beat a field that included Usada Pekora, Typical Gamer, Techno Gamerz and IlloJuan. He had also picked up multiple Best Variety Streamer awards at The Streamer Awards.For Baker, the win carried a very specific meaning. He had gone from long days of blue-collar maintenance work in a small Arkansas town to one of the biggest creator awards in gaming. His victory speeches repeatedly returned to that background, showing that the entire jump happened while he stayed rooted in the same story: an average guy from Arkansas finding a massive audience by being authentic and consistent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 200,000 visas could be revoked by the Trump administration. Here's who's affected and what happens next
articles.summary: The State Department is expected to announce the revocation of B-1 and B-2 visas issued over the past decade.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourist visas held by foreign nationals who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S., according to department documents obtained by the Associated Press .

The State Department is reportedly going to announce the action in the coming weeks. If the plans are carried out, it is believed it would represent the largest single mass visa revocation in U.S. history.

"We are coordinating with Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the Associated Press .

Here's what you need to know about what visas the government is targeting and what happens next.

The State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of B-1 and B-2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum.

Foreign nationals apply for a temporary B-1 visa or B-2 visa if they are visiting the U.S. for business or tourism.

Foreign nationals entering the country for business apply for B-1 visas to attend a business convention or conference, settle an estate, negotiate a contract or meet with business associates.

B-2 visas are for people visiting the U.S. on vacation. They would also apply for those seeing friends or relatives, seeking medical treatment, competing in amateur competitions or taking recreational courses that are not university-accredited.

Visa holders are usually let into the country for six months at a time. Border officers have some flexibility to admit someone for longer, up to a year, and if that's still not enough, people can apply to USCIS for a further extension, usually another six months.

Holding a B-1 or B-2 visa doesn't stop someone from applying for asylum. The two are entirely separate immigration processes, and doing one doesn't require or exclude the other.

However, when current applicants apply for a B-1 or B-2 visa, they are asked to confirm that they intend to return to their home country and are not planning to seek asylum, according to AP.

Under federal law , both immigrant and nonimmigrant visas can be revoked by the State Department at any time, including after someone has already traveled to the U.S.

Courts generally can't second-guess that decision, either. There's almost no way to challenge a visa revocation in court. The only exception is if someone is already in deportation proceedings and the revoked visa is the sole reason they're being removed, according to a Congressional Research Service report published in July.

If someone's B-1 or B-2 visa is revoked and they are already living in the U.S., if they leave the country for any reason, even briefly, they likely won't be allowed to re-enter. Their old visa would be void, so they'd have to apply for a new one from abroad, with no guarantee it would be approved.

Canceling someone's visa does not mean they will be immediately deported. Revoking a visa and deporting someone are two separate legal actions, handled by two different government agencies. The State Department can cancel a visa, but it takes a separate decision by the Department of Homeland Security to actually start the deportation process. Until that happens, the person isn't removed.

Someone whose visa is revoked doesn't lose every legal protection. If they're placed in deportation proceedings, they're still entitled to a hearing. That said, unlike in criminal cases, the government won't provide them a lawyer; they'd need to find one themselves or seek free legal aid.

People with pending claims could be recategorized but lose their status as business or tourism travelers, according to the AP report.

The State Department is expected to formally announce the plan in the coming weeks, though nothing is final yet. No policy has been published in the Federal Register, and officials have cautioned that both the scope and the process could still change before it's carried out.

Pigott, the State Department spokesperson, has said the process would be rolling rather than a single announcement: "As the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Legal challenges are widely expected. Courts have already pushed back on a related immigration move by the administration: a federal judge recently vacated Secretary of State Marco Rubio's suspension of immigrant visa processing from 75 countries, ruling it exceeded his statutory authority.

The Trump administration has so far revoked about 175,000 visas , the State Department said in August, the majority of which were due to "law enforcement encounters" such as assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug crimes. Overstays and public criticism of U.S. policy have also been cited as reasons .

A brief timeline of immigration actions since January 2025

Jan. 20, 2025: Trump returns to office and signs an executive order seeking to limit birthright citizenship , launching a broad immigration crackdown.

May 27, 2025: The State Department pauses new student visa interview appointments worldwide for F, M and J visas, as it moves to expand social media vetting.

June 4, 2025: A presidential proclamation bars full or partial entry to the U.S. from 19 countries.

Jan. 12, 2026: The State Department discloses the cumulative visa revocation total has surpassed 100,000 since Trump's inauguration, including about 8,000 student visas.

Jan. 14-21, 2026: The State Department announces a "full review" of screening policies , then pauses immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries.

Feb. 2, 2026: Plaintiffs sue Secretary of State Rubio over the 75-country visa pause.

June 30, 2026: The Supreme Court affirms birthright citizenship, striking down the president's Jan. 2025 order.

Aug. 6, 2026: Trump signs two executive orders in a new attempt to curtail birthright citizenship, despite June's Supreme Court ruling rejecting his previous effort.

Aug. 10, 2026: The State Department discloses the cumulative total of visas revoked has reached more than 175,000 since Trump's inauguration. This is at a pace of more than 10,000 revocations a month in 2026, up from about 8,000 a month in 2025.

Aug. 21, 2026: A federal judge vacates Rubio's 75-country visa pause , ruling it exceeded his statutory authority.

articles.title: Kennedy Center finances deteriorated sharply after Trump name change
articles.summary: Ticket sales and fundraising collapsed after President Donald Trump’s name was added to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, even as the cente...
articles.body:
Ticket sales and fundraising collapsed after President Donald Trump's name was added to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, even as the center's leaders publicly touted a financial turnaround, according to confidential documents obtained by The Washington Post.

Ticket sales had already dropped in the 10 months following Trump's takeover, but both ticket sales and donations plunged after the Trump-led board of trustees voted in December to rename the center after him and put his name on the front of the building, according to the records.

The documents show that leaders knew both were cratering even as they publicly portrayed Trump's takeover as a financial rescue. In a failed June request to keep Trump's name on the building, for instance, a Justice Department lawyer wrote that renaming the center after Trump "represented a saving of The Kennedy Center which, if this doesn't happen, would go into financial and structural collapse" - even suggesting in a new filing Monday that without Trump's name and renovation plan, the building "will be required to be taken down."

Just the week before the June filing, the center's own financial projections showed ticket revenue and fundraising had plummeted after the name change, putting it on track to fall nearly $100 million short of its revenue target.

The records - internal budgets, management forecasts, board minutes and financial presentations - provide the first comprehensive accounting of the center's financial deterioration in the year and a half since Trump replaced dozens of board members with allies and installed himself as chairman. Even after slashing expenses, center officials projected earned revenue this fiscal year to miss its budget target by 70 percent and contributed revenue to fall 25 percent short. The revenue miss was projected to leave the center with a $23 million deficit.

"The center took a huge hit when the takeover happened," and then appeared to stabilize, according to an official familiar with the center's financial situation. But after the name change, "it was just an absolute fiscal cliff. Donors disappeared, ticket sales disappeared, artists disappeared - like it was doomsday."

Andrew Taylor, director of American University's arts management program, who reviewed the documents at The Post's request, described the declines as "a nosedive."

Trump's takeover "had a consequence," Taylor said, "and the consequence was a catastrophic drop in revenue."

articles.title: Sanctions or missiles? How Gulf will view Trump’s new Iran approach
articles.summary: As Washington pressures Tehran, Gulf states weigh sanctions against the risk of escalation.
articles.body:
Nearly six months since the United States and Israel launched the first missiles in their war on Iran, Washington is pivoting to a strategy of tougher sanctions and economic isolation in a bid to force Tehran to accept its terms for a peace deal.

On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced “ Operation Economic Outcast ”, targeting Tehran’s remaining sources of revenue while also threatening penalties against those who continue doing business with Iran.

Bessent described the latest wave of sanctions as “the single greatest financial offensive ever” against Iran, and warned that banks and businesses would share in Iran’s isolation if they refuse to cooperate.

“No one is above the reach of US sanctions,” he told reporters.

Gulf states have repeatedly found themselves caught in the crosshairs during the US-Iran war as Iran has targeted US military assets and infrastructure in neighbouring countries.

Economic pressure may appear preferable to another round of US and Israeli missile strikes. But analysts warn the strategy carries its own risks, with Iran potentially responding to mounting economic pressure by targeting more US assets and energy infrastructure across the region.

Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said last week that if “any countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the strait of Hormuz”.

In peacetime, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas is shipped by Gulf producers through the critical waterway, which has become the main bone of contention in the war since Iran effectively closed it to shipping at the start of the war.

Iran’s stance leaves Washington’s Gulf allies facing an uncomfortable paradox: the US military presence helps protect them from Iranian missiles and drones, but also makes their territories potential targets.

Now, because of their security relationship with the United States, they are under increasing pressure to cut economic ties with Iran, which could provoke further Iranian retaliation and risk drawing them deeper into the conflict, experts say.

While the United Arab Emirates (UAE) moved last week to decisively cut economic ties with Iran, other Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Oman may have different strategic calculations to make. Analysts say they have strong incentives to preserve diplomatic channels with Tehran and to push for a deal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

From military offensive to ‘economic D-Day’

Bessent described the US measures aimed at isolating Iran as “economic D-Day”.

While the US and other countries have sanctioned Iran’s oil and financial sectors for decades, the latest wave will target five of Iran’s most important remaining economic lifelines: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.

Bessent also said Tehran’s trading partners are at risk of secondary sanctions if they continue helping turn Iranian oil into revenue. The Treasury imposed specific sanctions on 60 entities, vessels and individuals across the UAE, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and Switzerland, accusing them of facilitating Iranian trade.

But Iranian political analyst Mostafa Khoshcheschm dismissed the announcement as a “political show” intended to intimidate Iran’s neighbours.

He compared the campaign with Trump’s “maximum pressure” policy during his first term as US president, which was aimed at forcing Iran to renegotiate the US President Barack Obama-era Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) on its nuclear programme. That, Khoshcheschm noted, failed – ending with Trump withdrawing the US from the agreement instead in 2018.

The latest measures, the analyst argued, are “even weaker than that”.

The ramped-up emphasis on economic pressure comes as months of war have failed to produce a decisive outcome for the US, contrary to Trump’s indications at the start of the war that it would last for a matter of weeks. Meanwhile, US media reports that supplies of missiles and air defence interceptors in the Middle East may be running low – vehemently denied by the Trump administration – have incentivised Washington to pursue other means of pressuring Tehran, observers say.

The disruption to energy exports in the Strait of Hormuz has sent gas prices soaring in the US, making the war even more unpopular at home, even though efforts to establish alternative shipping routes have helped mitigate some of the economic fallout, experts say.

Despite this, Washington appears to believe the economic balance is in its favour. Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the US-based Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said Washington calculates that rerouting maritime traffic through Oman – combined with a wider shift away from Gulf oil – has reduced the effectiveness of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while the US blockade has sharply constrained Tehran’s ability to sell its oil.

“The result, in Washington’s view, is a status quo that imposes greater costs on Iran than on the United States,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

That calculation, he said, has led Trump to believe Washington can afford to wait Tehran out and that, for the first time since the war began, “time is working in America’s favour”.

But the effectiveness of this strategy may ultimately depend on whether major economies such as China, India and Russia believe Washington is prepared to impose meaningful penalties on them for continuing to trade with Iran.

Washington’s calculation may also be less comfortable for its Gulf allies. If the US believes it can withstand a prolonged economic war with Iran, it may be more willing to tolerate continued disruption in the Strait of Hormuz – a far more damaging prospect for Gulf economies heavily dependent on energy exports through the waterway.

That leaves Gulf states to calculate just how far they are willing to follow Washington’s economic campaign, particularly if doing so risks prolonging the confrontation with Tehran.

The UAE has already moved further than its Gulf neighbours, with Abu Dhabi saying last week it was ending trade with Iran.

Miad Maleki, an Iran analyst at the pro-Israel think tank the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said a comprehensive UAE financial and trade cutoff, if enforced, “may be the most consequential economic action of this war for Iran”, potentially exceeding the impact of the US embargo.

That’s because Dubai has long played an important role in Iran’s access to foreign currency, while the UAE has been Iran’s greatest source of imports even during the war.

Ultimately, though, the UAE has been hardest hit by Iran during the war with the US. It is also one of the few signatories to the US-led Abraham Accords, which seek to normalise relations between Israel and Arab states.

Simon Mabon, professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera the UAE’s position therefore reflects both its experience of Iranian attacks during the conflict and its increasingly close security relationship with Washington and Israel.

“The Emiratis are furious with Iran and they have taken a beating from Iran over the last few months,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. But he described the UAE as an “outlier” in the Gulf, adding he does not expect Saudi Arabia, Qatar or Oman to follow its lead.

Then there is the likely response from Iran.

Additional economic pressure may not produce the outcome Washington wants, analysts say.

“The pattern that we have seen so far is that when faced with either surrender or escalation, the Iranians escalate,” Parsi said.

With Bessent’s campaign aimed at forcing Tehran to capitulate or risk economic collapse, Parsi said escalation is “the most likely response” if the sanctions begin seriously hurting Iran, which retains “formidable escalatory options”.

That prospect is concerning for neighbours such as Qatar, where continued disruption to the Strait of Hormuz as well as strikes on its LNG operations have already inflicted economic pain. While alternative routes have allowed some oil exports to bypass the waterway, liquefied natural gas and many petrochemical products are harder to reroute.

Qatar has also supported mediation efforts and shares a vast gas field with Iran , giving Doha further incentive to preserve a functioning relationship with its neighbour.

Oman has its own reasons for resisting pressure to isolate Iran. Its longstanding role as an intermediary between Tehran and Washington depends on maintaining diplomatic channels with both sides. For one, it is locked in direct talks with Iran over the future management of the Strait of Hormuz.

Rashid al-Mohannad, vice president of the Doha-based Center for International Policy Research, said recent diplomatic activity, including a visit to Tehran by Oman’s foreign minister, “shows that there is a willingness from the mediating parties to try to pull both the US and Iran back to a diplomatic track”.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has taken a different approach, staying out of the recent mediation efforts while also showing little appetite for ramping up economic pressure on Tehran.

Mabon said that a decade ago, Riyadh might have been expected to follow Washington and Abu Dhabi in imposing tougher measures against Iran. Indeed, at one point the US seemed hopeful it could be persuaded to sign the Abraham Accords.

These days, Saudi has made a credible path towards the formalisation of a Palestinian state a condition for signing, which Israel refuses to accept. Furthermore, the kingdom has indicated an appetite for diversifying its security away from reliance on the US. To this end, it signed the Mecca Pact on mutual defence with Pakistan and Turkiye earlier this month.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also adopted a more pragmatic approach towards Tehran in recent years, culminating in the restoration of diplomatic relations under a China-brokered agreement in 2023.

Furthermore, while Riyadh may desire a weakened Iran, Mabon said, it is wary of the instability that could accompany the collapse of its government.

Joining Washington’s economic campaign could also further expose Saudi Arabia to attacks from Iran or the Iran-backed Houthis, which it has been fighting in Yemen and which are currently targeting Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea.

Restoring diplomacy between Tehran and Washington – something neither side seems able to do – has become increasingly essential for regional security.

That leaves Gulf capitals with a dilemma they cannot easily escape.

Going along with the US plan for economic pressure may appear preferable to another barrage of missiles. But joining Washington’s campaign could well provoke an Iranian response, raising the prospect of renewed attacks across the Gulf.

Gulf countries will likely continue to push hard for “dialogue and diplomacy” over renewed hostilities or tougher sanctions, which may ultimately be little more than yet another “gateway to further instability from Iran”.

articles.title: Nigeria kidnappings: President Bola Tinubu orders manhunt after victim video uploaded
articles.summary: The footage shows dozens of men, women and children sitting in a forest.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who launched deadly attacks on four villages in a remote part of Niger state last Friday.

Local residents told the BBC several mosques were simultaneously targeted during prayers. A local youth leader says as many as 500 people may have been abducted, though this has not been verified.

The president's orders came after the kidnappers posted a video on social media of what they said were those abducted last week sitting in a forest.

The authorities had previously suspected the attackers were bandits - criminal gangs involved in kidnapping and looting for ransom across parts of Nigeria.

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria

The gunmen, reportedly dressed in military-style clothing, attacked the villages of Dekara, Gidan Zana, Sabon Gida and Masaka.

Police spokesman Wasiu Abiodun told the BBC that more than 40 people were killed, but the exact number of deaths had not been confirmed.

Looking at the footage released on social media, the local youth leader, who asked not to be named, said he recognised several individuals from his community.

"I was able to identify many people. There is an elderly man in the video who is like a grandfather to us," he said. "He lives in Gidan Zana village."

He said families who had spotted relatives in the video were relieved to know they were still alive.

"At least they know where their loved ones are and hope they may be rescued, unlike those who still have no information about missing relatives," he added.

A local blogger familiar with the area told the BBC that many residents had fled their homes, seeking refuge in neighbouring states or across the border in Benin.

Some survivors are receiving hospital treatment, including people with serious injuries.

A local official also told the BBC that the attackers planted improvised explosive devices in parts of the affected communities as they led abductees into the forest. He said a teenage boy was killed when an explosive detonated as he tried to escape.

In a statement issued by presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga, Tinubu condemned the killings and abductions and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice.

"Those who carried out this cowardly attack on defenceless Nigerians are enemies of peace and enemies of humanity, who will not go scot-free," the statement said.

The president also expressed his condolences to the families of those killed.

The attack is the latest sign of worsening insecurity in the Borgu area, which borders Kebbi and Kwara states as well as neighbouring Benin.

Earlier this month, police said 145 people had been rescued after being abducted from four other villages in the area.

Local officials have also raised concerns about the growing presence of jihadist groups operating in parts of north-western Nigeria and along the border region, saying some fighters have recently entered communities and imposed religious restrictions on residents.

articles.title: 3-yr-oldâs rape-murder near Bihar border fuels death penalty debate in Nepal
articles.summary: South Asia News: NEW DELHI:  The rape and murder of a three-year-old girl in Nepalâs Bara district, around 25km from Raxaul in Bihar, triggered demands for the death p.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The rape and murder of a three-year-old girl in Nepalâs Bara district, around 25km from Raxaul in Bihar, triggered demands for the death penalty in parliament after days of protests, even as the principal suspect is a 16-year-old boy who, if convicted, would be sentenced under Nepalâs juvenile justice law. Lawmakers sought constitutional changes to allow capital punishment for heinous crimes, while RSP law minister Sobita Gautam and home minister Sudan Gurung told parliament that the govt could not introduce it without first amending the Constitution.The girl disappeared from Jeetpur-Simara on Aug 16 and her body was recovered two days later from an abandoned house near her home, leading to demonstrations in Simara, Kathmandu and other parts of Nepal. Police identified her teen neighbour as the principal suspect and widened the investigation, taking nine people into custody amid questions over whether officers had responded quickly enough after the family reported her missing.The killing dominated parliament proceedings, with ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Afsana Banu demanding an amendment to Article 16(2), which prohibits capital punishment, and calling for Nepal to reconsider its international commitments against the death penalty. âNo international treaty or law can stand above citizensâ safety. Concern for the human rights of criminals cannot come at the cost of victimsâ rights and justice,â she said, urging her govt to amend the Constitution to allow death penalty for heinous crimes.Other RSP lawmakers questioned whether the existing legal framework provided adequate punishment in such cases. Anushka Shrestha said, âA person should not escape severe punishment for a heinous crime merely because the perpetrator is a minor,â while arguing that punishment for rape needed review. Shraddha Kunwar raised a separate constitutional argument, asking whether parliament should focus only on the prohibition on death penalty or also ensure womenâs constitutional right to live with dignity.Gautam, however, told parliament that Article 16(2) explicitly barred Nepal from making any law providing for capital punishment and pointed to the country's international human rights commitments. âNo matter how intense public anger becomes, our govt cannot legislate beyond the Constitution,â she said. Nepal constitutionally abolished capital punishment in 1990 and retained the prohibition in its 2015 Constitution.The suspectâs age presents a separate legal issue even as lawmakers debate capital punishment. Under Nepalâs Children Act, 2018, anyone below 18 is dealt with under juvenile law, and an offender aged 16 to below 18 can receive two-thirds of the punishment prescribed for an adult. For adults, Nepalâs criminal law provides for imprisonment for the remainder of natural life for murder committed after rape, the maximum punishment available under the existing constitutional framework.Following days of protests, govt reached a three-point agreement with the victimâs family and formed a seven-member Garima Nyaya Sankalpa Samiti under law ministry, giving it seven days to recommend changes concerning sexual violence and offences against women and children.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: LASK to hold silence for Celtic fan who died during Champions League match
articles.summary: The 65-year-old supporter took ill during the first leg of the Champions League play-off in Glasgow last week.
articles.body:
Austrian champions LASK have held a silence in memory of a Celtic supporter who died when the sides met in Glasgow last week.

The 65-year-old fan became ill in the stadium during the first leg of the Champions League play-off at Celtic Park on Wednesday.

He was taken to Glasgow Royal Infirmary but died a short time later.

Ahead of the return leg in Linz - which kicked off at 20:00 - LASK confirmed they wished to pay tribute to the supporter.

O'Neill predicts 'tough old night' as Celtic take 3-0 lead to LASK

Duran scores twice as Celtic beat LASK to take big step towards Champions League

During the silence, fans held a banner that read: "Rest in peace, James".

Writing on social media, Celtic said: "LASK has contacted Celtic to advise that they wish to observe a period of silence prior to tonight's match in tribute to our supporter who fell ill and tragically passed away following last week's first leg at Celtic Park.

"We send our thanks and appreciation to LASK."

Last week Celtic thanked the emergency services and fellow fans for their efforts in dealing with the "tragic incident".

A club statement added: "We extend our deepest condolences, thoughts and prayers to the family and we will ensure that we offer them our full support at this extremely difficult time."

Martin O'Neill's team hold a 3-0 advantage going into the match at the Raiffeisen Arena.

The winner will progress to the lucrative group stage of the Champions League.

articles.title: Sunderland University relocated gallery set for first exhibition
articles.summary: The Northern Gallery for Contemporary Art opens in September after the closure of the Glass Centre.
articles.body:
The first exhibition of an art gallery forced to move to new premises has been announced.

The Northern Gallery for Contemporary Art (NGCA) is moving to the Culture House in Sunderland on 12 September, opening with an exhibition on local artist Audrey Amiss.

The University of Sunderland, which runs the gallery, said Kitchen Sink Realism would feature previously unseen paintings and drawings, as well as archival material by the late Sunderland-born artist.

The gallery was previously housed at the National Glass Centre, which shut in July after the university said it could not afford building repairs.

Despite being a prolific artist, it was only after her death in 2013 that Amiss' breadth of work came to light.

She is known for her campaigning against harmful treatment in the mental health system, after a crisis she suffered as a student in the 1950s.

Her exhibition will be on display until 17 January, and the university is offering printmaking workshops on the opening weekend.

Kevin Petrie, professor of creative practice at the university, said the gallery was a "long-standing asset" for students.

"It gives them the chance to work alongside the exhibition curator, and in many cases artists themselves, to learn first-hand about careers and professional practice in the arts," he said.

Culture House will also house a library, podcasting studios and a sky garden when it opens.
