articles.title: Jimmy Donaldson started YouTube at 13; years later the channel became the foundation of a $5 billion global business
articles.summary: US Streamers News: At just 13, Jimmy Donaldson was already uploading videos under the name âMrBeast6000â from Eastern North Carolina. What started with low-view uploads .
articles.body: At just 13, Jimmy Donaldson was already uploading videos under the name âMrBeast6000â from Eastern North Carolina. What started with low-view uploads while he was still dealing with school eventually became something much bigger than a YouTube channel. Donaldson spent years studying what made videos work, and that obsession became the base for a business empire now known as Beast Industries. The strange part is how long the early grind lasted. From 2012 to 2016, he uploaded hundreds of videos without huge numbers. During his late teens, he also spent hours on Skype with a small group of other creators. They would break down YouTube recommendations, test thumbnail layouts, compare titles and study how long viewers stayed on videos. Basically, the platform itself became their experiment.The system Jimmy Donaldson built before the big breakthroughThe big shift came in January 2017, when Donaldson posted a video of himself counting to 100,000. It took around 40 hours to complete, but the stunt helped turn him into a much bigger name.His approach to money was also pretty different. Instead of simply keeping early advertising income, Donaldson pushed it straight back into new videos. The system was simple: if one video made $10,000, he would spend $10,000 on the next one.That reinvestment kept raising the scale. Small cash giveaways eventually became elaborate sets, real islands and huge survival-style productions. Each project was built to become bigger than the previous one.From YouTube creator to Beast IndustriesVideo alone was never the final destination. Donaldson moved into consumer products, with Feastables becoming a major part of the operation. The snack brand went on to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in retail sales around the world.Beast Industries also moved into areas far outside traditional creator businesses. The company acquired teen-focused fintech platform Step and launched Beast Mobile, pushing the operation into finance and telecom.By this point, the YouTube channel was feeding a much larger corporate structure. Beast Industries, led by CEO Jeffrey Housenbold, is valued at roughly $5.2 billion, according to the information provided.MrBeastâs biggest milestones are now happening at massive scaleDonaldson later pushed the brand into television-style entertainment through Beast Games, a reality competition series made with Amazon Prime Video and backed by a huge production budget.The scale of the original channel also kept climbing. MrBeast overtook T-Series in June 2024 and then reached another major milestone on June 12, 2026, becoming the first YouTube channel to pass 500 million subscribers.His estimated net worth is around $2.6 billion, with much of that value tied to private-company equity. TIME also placed the operation on its TIME100 Most Influential Companies list. The story has moved far beyond a teenager uploading from North Carolina. articles.title: Archaeologists found 9,000-year-old arrowheads covered in strange markings; their purpose remains a mystery
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For nearly nine thousand years, a set of Anatolian arrowheads has been quietly guarding a secret. Archaeologists working at Tepecik-Ciftlik, a Neolith.
articles.body: For nearly nine thousand years, a set of Anatolian arrowheads has been quietly guarding a secret. Archaeologists working at Tepecik-Ciftlik, a Neolithic settlement in Cappadocia, central Turkey, have identified eleven newly recognised obsidian points bearing deliberate, hand-cut incisions, bringing the site's total to twelve and the wider regional count to 54. According to the study published in PLOS One, titled âIntentional incisions on Neolithic Obsidian arrowheads from Central Anatolia: A techno-functional and iconographic approachâ, these markings were made on purpose, not left by accident during manufacture or centuries buried in the ground. Yet despite careful microscopic analysis, experimental replication and comparison with dozens of similar finds across Central Anatolia, the arrowheads' meaning remains stubbornly out of reach. Were they hunters' signatures, decorative flourishes, or something closer to ritual? No two designs match, and the practice never spread beyond this one corner of the ancient world, leaving researchers with more questions than answers.9,000-year-old Neolithic arrowheads in Turkey show mysterious incised symbolsThese arrowheads are not distinguished by their shape or size, which match the ordinary points found alongside them, but by the presence of small, hand-cut lines etched into their ventral faces, crosses, chevrons, wavy lines, squares, and an occasional letter-like form. Microscopic examination ruled out accidental scratching. The researchers established three criteria for genuine incisions, namely visibility to the naked eye, clear removal of material, and evidence of repeated, controlled strokes, and on that basis confirmed intentional marks on ten of the twelve pieces, with two remaining ambiguous.No two designs are identical, and the number of strokes required ranges from a single cut to twenty on the most elaborate specimen, arrowhead 4, whose three linked squares took repeated passes to complete. The corpus shows "no correlation with raw material, chaÃ®ne opÃ©ratoire, typology, or use-wear." In other words, whatever drove someone to mark a particular point, it wasn't linked to how the tool was made or used.Flint tools were used to carve markings into obsidian arrowheadsTo understand the technique, the team ran an experiment, attempting to incise a fresh obsidian blade with both a flint tool and another piece of obsidian. Obsidian proved too soft to mark obsidian effectively, whereas a flint edge, harder on the Mohs scale, cut clean, deliberate lines. That is notable because flint makes up under one per cent of the site's stone tools, suggesting its use here was a considered choice rather than convenience.The timing of the incisions relative to each arrowhead's shaping proved just as inconsistent as everything else. In three cases the cuts were made before the final retouching, in three others afterwards, and in six the sequence could not be determined at all. Functionally, the picture is similarly murky: only one incised point, arrowhead 11, showed a fracture consistent with having struck a target, while the rest bore no clear signs of use as projectiles, ruling neither hunting nor purely symbolic purposes in or out.Why Neolithic communities in Turkey carved mysterious markings into arrowheadsThe mystery isn't confined to Tepecik-Ciftlik. Similar incised arrowheads have turned up at ÃatalhÃ¶yÃ¼k, Can Hasan III, KÃ¶mÃ¼rcÃ¼-Kaletepe and a handful of other Cappadocian and Konya Plain sites, and the study notes intriguing formal echoes between them, such as a cross at Tepecik-Ciftlik resembling one from ÃatalhÃ¶yÃ¼k, and wavy-line motifs matching pieces from Can Hasan III. Yet Cappadocian obsidian itself travelled far beyond the region, as far as the southern Levant, without carrying the incising tradition with it, which the authors argue points to "specific cultural practices confined to certain Neolithic communities."The leading theory, first proposed by archaeologist Kathryn Ataman in 1988 after studying arrowheads from Can Hasan III, was that the marks functioned as hunters' signatures, a way of claiming a kill, drawing loosely on ethnographic parallels from Inuit hunting groups. Comparing the Anatolian finds against incised projectiles from Iron Age Phoenicia, Bronze Age Mesopotamia and Palaeolithic Europe turned up no close parallel, leading the pair to conclude only that decoration, ownership marks and something closer to ritual or magical practice all remain plausible.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Spain requests emergency funding from the EU over Ceuta migrants
articles.summary: European Commission says it is ‘assessing’ Spain’s request after some 70,000 migrants surged into North African enclave.
articles.body:
Spain has formally requested emergency funding from the European Union to address the migration situation in its North African enclave of Ceuta, weeks after tens of thousands of people surged across the border from Morocco.

The European Commission said on Tuesday that it is closely monitoring the situation and remained “fully engaged at all levels” to ensure the security of the EU’s external borders.

Commission spokesman Markus Lammert said during a daily news briefing in Brussels, “We have now, namely yesterday, received a formal request for emergency funding, and we are now working on assessing their request as a priority and with a view to taking a swift decision.”

This comes after more than 70,000 would-be migrants, driven by poverty and misinformation, rushed towards Ceuta at the end of July, in one of the deadliest migration crises to hit the region.

At least 90 people died on both sides of the border, according to official numbers, while human rights groups reported higher figures.

The Spanish government also took steps to speed up the return of the migrants who still remain in the Spanish territory of Ceuta.

Most of them have since returned to Morocco, but between five percent and 10 percent – between 3,500 and 7,000 people – remain in Ceuta, including unaccompanied children who cannot be deported.

Spanish authorities must identify those remaining in Ceuta to establish whether they are entitled to international protection or, if not, begin procedures for their return.

The process has been criticised as too slow by Ceuta’s regional government, which is controlled by the conservative Popular Party (PP).

To speed up the response, Spain’s cabinet on Tuesday approved the creation of a “single command” for Ceuta, to be led by Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres.

The priority is “the return and repatriation of the greatest possible number of people, adults and minors”, while respecting Spanish law and human rights, Torres told reporters after the cabinet approved the measure.

While return procedures are accelerated, the government will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to those who seek asylum or are unaccompanied minors and therefore cannot be returned, he added.

Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s two North African enclaves, hold the EU’s only land borders with Africa.

Both enclaves operate under a special arrangement within the Schengen free-travel zone, which requires anyone crossing in to face border checks before continuing onward to mainland Spain.
